source_text: Confodiuntur nempe Manichaei, et peccatum naturale credentes, et resurrectionem carnis negantes. Nunc autem - inquit - Christus resurrexit a mortuis primitiae dormientium; quoniam quidem per hominem mors, et per hominem resurrectio mortuorum [n214] . De resurrectione hic Apostolus non generali loquitur, quam experturi sunt etiam scelesti, etiam profani homines; sed de eorum tantummodo, qui transferentur in gloriam. Beatam ergo resurrectionem puro nomine resurrectionis ostendit, cuius comparatione, illa impiorum quasi non sit resurrectio, praeteritur. Hic ergo Apostolus non solum resurrectionem, ut dixi, quae bonis malisque communis est, sed resurrectionem inculcat beatam; et licet non sit unum resurrectio et beatitudo resurrectionis, sicut nec resurrectio et resurrectionis miseria unum est; tamen quia beatitudo aeterna absque resurrectione non est, nomine eius illa quoque felicitas, quae excitationem haud paenitendam facit esse, signatur. Ut si aliquis industriam, vires, et studia diversa collaudans, compendio ea vitae velit ostendere, verbi gratia, eruditam illius vitam, elegantem huius, impigram appellet alterius; non utique amoverit distinctionem, ut idem vita quod industria, quod elegantia, quod fortitudo videatur; aliud est quippe vivere, aliud studere; verumtamen nisi vixeris, nullus studebis. Ita etiam non est idem resurrectio quod beatitudo; est quippe misera excitatio cinerum; tamen nullus regnabis, nisi ante resurrexeris. Mors ergo corporis et resurrectio corporis e regione consistunt; si mors esset universa poenalis, esset quoque universa resurrectio praemialis; nunc autem est resurrectio poenalis omnium, qui ignibus deputantur aeternis; ergo et mors non supplicialis est, sed naturalis. Sicut enim non facit generaliter mors corporis, ut paeniteat interiisse; sic non facit generaliter resurrectio, ut placeat revixisse. Verum et istius bonum in remuneratione surgentium, et illius amaritudo in adustione punitorum est; quae utraque pro meritis consequuntur. Apparet igitur Apostolum non de morte naturali, sed de criminosorum, quam infelicem facit poena perpetua; nec de resurrectione communi, sed quam beatam facit gloria sempiterna, disserere; nec ubi de personis disputat praeiudicium inferre creaturis, sed salvis semper distinctionibus latisque limitibus naturarum et voluntatum, sic miscere nonnumquam vocabula, ne specialitas rerum confusione depereat. Per hominem ergo mors, et per hominem resurrectio mortuorum: non hic ab homine morte conditam; sed in homine apparuisse denuntiat; sicut et resurrectionem mortuorum non dicit ab homine factam, hoc est, a Christo; sed in homine, sicut ad Philippenses idem magister: Oboediens - inquit - factus est usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis; propter quod et Deus illum exaltavit, et donavit illi nomen super omne nomen [n215] . Petri quoque apostoli in hoc concurrit assertio: Viri Israelitae, audite: Iesum virum Nazarenum approbatum a Deo in vobis per manus iniquorum interemistis, quem Deus suscitavit solutis doloribus inferni. Et item: Hunc Iesum Deus resuscitavit, cui omnes nos testes sumus [n216] . Ibi ergo sicut proprium erat hominis sine deitatis iniuria obire mortem, ita proprium divinitatis hominem illum a mortuis excitare. Quod autem Deus pronuntiatur operari ex persona Verbi, ipse quoque Christus facit. Sic enim dixerat: In potestate habeo ponere animam meam, et in potestate habeo sumere illam [n217] . Cum ergo sit Filii una persona, tamen distinctione legitima aliud applicatur carni, aliud deitati. Per hominem ergo mors, et per hominem resurrectio mortuorum, manifestata, non creata; ceterum utrumque institutum per Deum est; sed in Adam mortis conditio, in persona vero Christi primitiae resurrectionis claruerunt. Hic ergo ubi dicit Apostolus: Per hominem mors; si per voluntatem eius dicas, nihil pertinet ad naturam; si per naturam, nihil spectat ad culpam. Homines nempe alterum mortis, alterum resurrectionis ex adverso locavit, istum secundum nolens illi subdere. Et sequitur: Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita et in Christo omnes vivificabuntur. Hoc ergo quod ait: Omnes in Christo vivificabuntur, etiam de impiis, an tantum de fidelibus dicit? Si de impiis, quod omnes vivificentur in Christo, ergo nullus in poena est; si de fidelibus, non ergo universi vivificantur in fide Christi, sed tantum fideles, quamvis omnes omnino virtute ipsius, qua conditi fuerant, excitentur. Si ergo de morte corporis loquitur: In Adam omnes moriuntur, nullus hoc nomine indicatur reatus, quando in eodem Adam et Christus mortuus invenitur; neque enim secuta esset veritas resurrectionis, nisi praecessisset veritas mortis. Igitur in Adam pronuntiat Apostolus omnes mori. Si haec mors non indicat aliud quam corporis resolutionem; nihil spectat profecto ad naturale peccatum, nec quidquam praeiudicat innocentibus, si in Adam mori dicantur, in quo et Christus est mortuus. Sin autem hoc quod ait: In Adam omnes moriuntur, ad peccatum vis animi, et non ad mortem solum, sed ad mortem ream et miseram pertinere, id est, quam deputata criminibus poena consequitur; in ea autem videlicet gehenna nec Christus potuit esse, nec sancti; igitur nec innocentibus praeiudicat, qui ut nihil boni, ita nihil mali voluntarii habent; sed hoc solum retinent, quod a Deo facti sunt; quos iure Baptismatis consecramus, ut qui eos fecit condendo bonos, faciat innovando et adoptando meliores. Quod itaque dicit Apostolus: Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita et in Christo omnes vivificabuntur; abest tantum ab ista suspicione traducis Manichaeae, quantum Christus a peccato, qui et iniquitatem non habuit, et minus de hominis natura nihil habuit.
pass_a_gloss: The Manichaeans are indeed pierced, both those believing a natural sin, and those denying a resurrection of the flesh. But now, he says, Christ rose from the dead firstfruits of those sleeping; because indeed through a human death, and through a human a resurrection of the dead. The Apostle here speaks not of a general resurrection, which even the wicked, even profane humans will experience; but of those only who will be transferred into glory. He therefore shows a blessed resurrection by the pure name of resurrection, by whose comparison that of the impious, as if it were not a resurrection, is passed over. Here therefore the Apostle impresses not only a resurrection, as I said, which is common to good and evil, but a blessed resurrection; and although resurrection and the blessedness of resurrection are not one, as neither resurrection and the misery of resurrection are one; nevertheless because eternal blessedness is not without resurrection, by its name that happiness also, which makes an excitation not to be repented, is marked. As if someone praising industry, powers, and diverse studies, would want by a shortcut to show them of life, for example, he would call that one's life erudite, this one's elegant, another's unslothful; he would not indeed have removed a distinction, so that life would seem the same as industry, as elegance, as fortitude; for it is one thing to live, another to study; nevertheless unless you have lived, you will study as no one. So also resurrection is not the same as blessedness; for there is a miserable excitation of ashes; yet you will reign as no one, unless you have first risen. The death of the body therefore and the resurrection of the body stand from the opposite side; if death were universally penal, resurrection also would be universally of reward; but now there is a penal resurrection of all who are assigned to eternal fires; therefore death also is not of punishment, but natural. For as the death of the body does not generally make that one repent to have perished; so resurrection does not generally make that it please to have lived again. But both the good of this is in the remuneration of those rising, and the bitterness of that in the burning of the punished; which both follow according to deserts. It appears therefore that the Apostle discusses not about a natural death, but about that of the criminal, which a perpetual penalty makes unhappy; nor about a common resurrection, but which an everlasting glory makes blessed; nor where he disputes about persons does he bring a prior judgment upon creatures, but the distinctions of natures and of wills always remaining safe and the limits broad, he so sometimes mixes words, lest the speciality of things perish by confusion. Through a human therefore death, and through a human a resurrection of the dead: he denounces here not death founded by a human; but that it appeared in a human; as he also does not say a resurrection of the dead was made by a human, that is, by Christ; but in a human, as to the Philippians the same teacher: He was made, he says, obedient even to death, but death of the cross; on account of which God also exalted him, and gave him a name above every name. The assertion of Peter the apostle also concurs in this: Men of Israel, hear: Jesus a man of Nazareth approved by God among you through the hands of the unjust you killed, whom God raised, the pains of hell having been loosed. And likewise: This Jesus God resuscitated, of whom we all are witnesses. There therefore as it was proper of a human to go to death without injury of deity, so it was proper of divinity to stir that human from the dead. But what God is pronounced to work from the person of the Word, Christ himself also does. For thus he had said: I have it in power to lay down my soul, and I have it in power to take it. When therefore there is one person of the Son, nevertheless by a legitimate distinction another thing is applied to the flesh, another to the deity. Through a human therefore death, and through a human a resurrection of the dead, manifested, not created; for the rest each was instituted through God; but in Adam the condition of death, but in the person of Christ the firstfruits of resurrection became clear. Here therefore where the Apostle says: Through a human death; if you say through his will, it pertains nothing to nature; if through nature, it looks nothing to fault. He placed humans, one of death, another of resurrection from the opposite, unwilling to subjoin this second to that. And it follows: As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive. This therefore which he says: All will be made alive in Christ, does he say even of the impious, or only of the faithful? If of the impious, that all will be made alive in Christ, therefore no one is in penalty; if of the faithful, not therefore are all made alive in the faith of Christ, but only the faithful, although all altogether are stirred by his virtue, by which they had been founded. If therefore he speaks of the death of the body: In Adam all die, no guilt is indicated by this name, when in the same Adam even Christ is found dead; for a truth of resurrection would not have followed, unless a truth of death had gone before. Therefore in Adam the Apostle pronounces all die. If this death indicates nothing other than a resolution of the body; it looks indeed nothing to a natural sin, nor does it prejudge innocents anything, if they are said to die in Adam, in whom even Christ died. But if this which he says: In Adam all die, you want to belong to a charge of the mind, and not to death only, but to a guilty and miserable death, that is, which a penalty assigned to charges follows; but in that gehenna namely neither Christ could be, nor the holy; therefore it does not prejudge innocents, who as they have nothing of good, so nothing of voluntary evil; but they retain this only, that they were made by God; whom we consecrate by the right of Baptism, so that he who made them good by founding may make them better by renewing and adopting. What therefore the Apostle says: As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive; is as far from that suspicion of a Manichaean tradux as Christ from sin, who both did not have iniquity, and had nothing less of the human's nature.

pass_b_english: The Manichaeans are surely pierced through, both for believing natural sin and for denying flesh’s resurrection. ‘But now,’ he says, ‘Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep. Since death came through a human being, resurrection of the dead also comes through a human being’ (1 Corinthians 15:20–21) (Romans 9:11). Here the apostle speaks not of the general resurrection, which even criminals and impious people will experience, but only of those to be transferred into glory. He indicates blessed resurrection by the unqualified name ‘resurrection,’ passing over the ungodly’s rising as though, compared with it, it were no resurrection at all.

Here, then, as I said, the apostle stresses not simply resurrection, common to good and evil people, but blessed resurrection. Resurrection and the blessedness of resurrection are not the same thing, just as resurrection and the misery of resurrection are not the same. Yet because eternal blessedness does not exist without resurrection, its name also indicates the happiness that makes being raised no cause for regret.

For example, someone praising industry, strength, and diverse pursuits may wish to describe them briefly under the heading of life: calling one person’s life learned, another’s elegant, another’s energetic. This certainly does not remove the distinction, as though life were identical with industry, elegance, or strength. Living is one thing, striving another; nevertheless you cannot strive unless you live. Likewise resurrection is not identical with blessedness—there is a miserable raising of ashes—but you will not reign unless you first rise.

Bodily death and bodily resurrection therefore stand opposite each other. If every death were penal, every resurrection would also be a reward. But the resurrection of all who are assigned to eternal fire is penal; therefore death too need not be punishment, but is natural. Just as bodily death does not in every case make dying regrettable, resurrection does not in every case make returning to life delightful. The good in the latter lies in the reward of those rising, and the bitterness in the former in the burning of those punished; both follow according to deserts.

It is therefore clear that the apostle discusses not natural death but the death of criminals, made unhappy by perpetual punishment; not common resurrection but the resurrection made blessed by everlasting glory. Where he discusses persons he does not prejudice created natures. He always preserves the distinctions and broad boundaries of natures and wills, sometimes combining terms without letting confusion destroy the particular character of things.

‘Death through a human being, and resurrection of the dead through a human being’: he does not announce here that death was created by a human, but appeared in a human. Likewise he does not say resurrection was effected by a human—that is, by Christ as human—but in a human. So the same teacher says to the Philippians: ‘He became obedient to death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name above every name’ (Philippians 2:8–9).

The apostle Peter’s assertion agrees: ‘People of Israel, listen: Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God among you, you killed through the hands of the wicked. God raised him, releasing the pains of the underworld.’ Again: ‘God raised this Jesus, of whom we are all witnesses’ (Acts 2:22–24, 32). There it belonged to humanity to undergo death without injury to divinity, and to divinity to raise that man from the dead. Yet what God is declared to do, Christ himself also does in the person of the Word. For he had said: ‘I have power to lay down my life, and power to take it up’ (John 10:18). Although the Son is one person, a proper distinction attributes one thing to flesh, another to divinity.

Death through a human, then, and resurrection of the dead through a human: manifested, not created. Both were established by God. But death’s condition became evident in Adam, and resurrection’s firstfruits in Christ’s person. Here, where the apostle says, ‘Death through a human,’ if you mean through his will, it concerns no nature; if through nature, it concerns no fault. He placed two human beings opposite one another, one associated with death, the other with resurrection, refusing to subordinate the second to the first.

It follows: ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ’ (1 Corinthians 15:22). Does ‘All will be made alive in Christ’ include the ungodly, or refer only to believers? If to the ungodly, because everyone is made alive in Christ, no one is punished. If to believers, then not everyone is made alive in Christ’s faith, but only believers, although absolutely everyone is raised by the same power through which they were created.

If he speaks of bodily death—‘All die in Adam’—this name indicates no guilt, since Christ too is found to have died in that same Adam. The reality of resurrection would not have followed unless the reality of death came first. The apostle therefore pronounces that all die in Adam. If this death indicates nothing other than bodily dissolution, it plainly concerns no natural sin and prejudices no innocent people: they are said to die in Adam, in whom Christ also died.

But if you want ‘All die in Adam’ to concern sin of the soul—not mere death, but guilty and miserable death, followed by the punishment assigned to crimes—then neither Christ nor the saints could be in that Gehenna. It therefore prejudices no innocent people either, who possess no voluntary evil just as they possess no voluntary good, but have only this: they were made by God. We consecrate them through baptism’s rite, so that the one who made them good by creating them may make them better by renewing and adopting them. Thus the apostle’s saying, ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ,’ is as far from the suspicion of Manichaean inherited sin as Christ is from sin: he possessed no iniquity, yet lacked nothing of human nature.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
